title: Example (v): ∫₀^∞ x^{n-1} dx / ∏_{k≥0}(1+a^k x) and triangular-number identity
note: Surface notation involves a q-Pochhammer-like product. But Ramanujan does NOT use (a;q)_n notation, D_q, Heine, or the q-binomial theorem. He treats the product as an ordinary Taylor series in x and reduces to Master Theorem. So this does NOT trigger the schema's q_shift detector (correctly: the operator move is Master Theorem, not q-shift).
berndt_nb1_entry_ref: NB II Ch. 4 Entry 13.8 (sinh/sinh product family — Berndt p. 107 Entry 13: explicit cos integral derived from Master Theorem; cited by Berndt p. 302 as the same integral Ramanujan published in [13]); the triangular-number identity is due to Gauss (Andrews [1 p. 23] per Berndt p. 303)

berndt_nb1_entry_ref: Not found in NB Ch. 3-4; Berndt p. 312 treats this section as a standalone numerical application of the (2.11) expansion (which itself derives from Master Theorem). The cube-roots-of-unity transcendental-root computation is QR-specific.

title: §4: Theorem II — Frullani-extended Master Theorem
note: The Frullani-limit move (n→0 in a Master-Theorem identity) is a distinct operator. The 6-operator schema does not capture this specific limit, though MASTER_THEOREM itself is the underlying primitive.
berndt_nb1_entry_ref: Berndt p. 314 explicit and emphatic: 'However none of these papers contains Ramanujan's beautiful Theorem II which evidently has not heretofore appeared in the literature.' Theorem II is the strongest GENUINELY_NOVEL flag in the entire QR corpus per Berndt's own annotations. Not in NB Ch. 3-4.

title: §5: Examples of Theorem II — Frullani as special case
berndt_nb1_entry_ref: Direct applications of the Theorem-II novelty above. Not in NB Ch. 3-4. (Some special cases reduce to Frullani's classical theorem; the four QR examples (2.17)/(i)-(iv) extend this to the (1+ax)^{-p} - (1+bx)^{-q} pattern.)

berndt_nb1_entry_ref: NB II Ch. 4 Entry 11 Cors 1-4 (Berndt p. 318 explicit: 'Corollary (ii) is simply (1.4) and is also found in Chapter 4 Section 11 Corollary 1'; p. 319: 'Corollary (v) is also found in Chapter 4 Section 11 Corollary 3'; p. 319: 'Corollary (vii) is Corollary 4 in Section 11 of Chapter 4'). Section §6 is essentially the QR rederivation of Ch. 4 §11 Cors 1-4.

title: §7: Theorem III — Fourier cosine/sine self-reciprocity
note: This is the Fourier cosine inversion theorem (modern: F_c·F_c = π/2·Id). It is NOT one of the 6 predicted operators. The 6-operator MELLIN_INVERSION is conceptually similar (continuous transform self-inverse) but the schema's regex looks for Mellin-specific signatures (x^{s-1}, Bromwich, Γ(s)) — Fourier cos has none of these.
berndt_nb1_entry_ref: NB II Ch. 4 Entry 12 (Berndt p. 107 Entry 12: 'The first part of Entry 12 gives the inversion formula for Fourier cosine transforms... We defer Ramanujan's proof until our examination of the quarterly reports'). Theorem III is the QR-extended version of NB Ch. 4 Entry 12(i).

title: Examples of Theorem III + closing integrals
berndt_nb1_entry_ref: Standard applications of Fourier cos pair (Ex 1: 1/(1+x²) → e^{-n}; etc.). The basic identities are in NB Ch. 4 §13 / standard tables (Gradshteyn-Ryzhik); the Fresnel-like Ex 4 (cos(π/4 - a/x)/√x against cos nx) is more exotic. Berndt p. 323 notes the absolute-non-integrability caveat: 'cos(2√(ax))/√x is not absolutely integrable on [0 ∞) and so the aforementioned theorem in Titchmarsh's text... cannot be applied. Nonetheless these two evaluations are correct as can be verified from results in Gradshteyn and Ryzhik.'

title: §1: Validity of Theorem I revisited — nature of u_n
§2-§3: Uniqueness of the function passing through u_n
note: This is a meta-discussion about interpolation, important as a foundation for all subsequent fractional-iteration / fractional-differentiation work but not itself an operator move.

title: §4-§5: Fractional Order of Functions — definition of F^n
note: This is the entry point to Ramanujan's fractional iteration theory. Closely related to the Schröder / Koenig functional equation tradition. Not in the 6-operator schema.

title: §6: Conjugation theorem for fractional iteration + examples
note: Schröder conjugation: F^n acts on a fixed-point-free function by conjugating to a 'normal form' φ where the iterate is easy (a power map). Example (b) — F(x) = x²-2 has the Chebyshev semigroup as its iteration; F^{log 3/log 2}(x) = x³-3x and so on, which Ramanujan computes explicitly.

title: §7: Orders of Infinity — Hardy ≺ notation
§8: Construction of a function defying all logarithmic scales
§9: Scales of Orders of Infinity — theorem that the number of scales is infinite
§10: Expand f^r(x) in ascending powers of r — derives ψ_1(x) = C/F(x)
note: This is the Lie-theoretic / generator-of-flow content of fractional iteration. Modern: ψ_1 is the vector field of the iteration flow.

title: §11: Fractional Order of Differentiation
note: This is the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative via the Cauchy formula, but with the role of f and its derivatives flipped (operates on f^{(r)}, returns f^{(r-n)}). Has a Mellin-style kernel x^{n-1} but is not what schema mellin_inversion detects; the schema looks for x^{s-1} F(x) where F is a function, not f^{(r)}.

title: §12: The Use of Operators — shift E, difference Δ
note: Heaviside / umbral operator calculus. The MASTER_THEOREM appears here AS A CHECK / consistency test: substituting E for a scalar a in the Mellin integral gives back the Master Theorem statement. Methodologically interesting — Ramanujan is using the Master Theorem as a check on his operator calculus.

title: §13: Partial fractions of an infinite product → cos integrals
§14: Finite-vs-infinite Fourier — discontinuous-bandwidth theorem
note: The bandlimited variant of Theorem III. This is essentially the Paley-Wiener phenomenon: compactly-supported φ has Fourier transform that 'looks band-pass' against trial functions.

title: §15: Reciprocal-pair theorem — Mellin pair self-reciprocity + Bessel/Fourier corollaries
note: Most general reciprocity theorem in the QRs. Uses MASTER_THEOREM in the proof (line 5234, line 5275) but the *operator* is Mellin-pair reciprocity — a generalization of Mellin self-inversion to pairs of functions.
